title: Appendix G — Specification and design decisions
text:
1.1 Goal
Build the full Python model (“Coded CPAT”) that directly replicates the mitigation and distribution modules of Excel-AI (excel_ai/CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm, CPAT-AI-Distribution-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm). The numbers must match Excel-AI. The overall norm is: always follow Excel-AI. Where an Excel-AI choice looks strange or wrong, report it to the user rather than silently departing; known departures from legacy CPAT are already tracked in the register (bugs L, issues I, departures LD, upgrades U).
The purpose of the code is full human readability: a reader with the methodology in one hand should be able to find each equation in the code in the other.


1.2 Ways the model is run

From saved scenarios: a table of scenario inputs in the MTInputs form (one row per NameOfParameter, one column per scenario), as legacy CPAT and Excel-AI ScenarioDefinition.
From a reactive Shiny user interface (later), which populates the same inputs dynamically.
Both use an advanced inputs file as well: time series and longer-form inputs of different types (the legacy Manual inputs tab).

The code runs many countries and many scenarios in one call (batch, comparisons), and one country with two or more scenarios (the main user interface).


1.3 Data: databases
Python and Excel-AI both run from the same databases. A database holds two or more complete sets of data:








Set
Contents
Where




Full
Every table, including the four proprietary tables
A separate, private repository (never this one)


Public
Every table except the four proprietary tables: energy balances (EnergyCons/Balances), domestic prices (Prices_dom), the GTAP input-output table (IO_GTAP) and the household survey (HHSurvey)
This repository (data/)



This mirrors how Excel-AI and legacy CPAT work (legacy NoPropData workbooks lack the same four tables).


1.4 Testing

Compare Python with Excel-AI systematically.
Compare Python or Excel-AI with legacy CPAT.
In each case first for one country, then for all.
For these comparisons use a systematic dataset: the public set (full except the four proprietary tables), with the four tables filled the same way in every model.



1.5 Documentation and readability

The methodology is in docs/01_MainDocumentation/*.qmd. A website will be built from qmd (to HTML), with tabs for Excel-AI and for Python.
Plan the Python project in a human-readable way too, in qmd (markdown with extras) that can be built into the website and into Word.
An equation list: an executive summary with the core equations of each part, and appendices with all the adjustments. It uses the Greek letters and index letters of the methodology documentation; indices are shown only where they add clarity (otherwise the text says which indices an equation ranges over).
A parallel version with code names instead of Greek letters, using the authoritative list of CPAT variable codes (e.g. ener), the codes map in excel_ai/.
Box diagrams of the modular structure.
A separate NORMS and TODO for the Python project. Most Excel norms (formatting) do not apply; the overriding norm is to follow Excel-AI.



1.6 Structure

Decide up front whether the model computes everything for year t (all modules, including air pollution and transport co-benefits) before moving to year t+1.
Placeholder modules for air pollution and transport co-benefits, with their imports and exports defined now. Transport co-benefits will later be related to the transport (engineer) mitigation model.
Switchable core equations. The structure must allow later switching between forms of the core equations through one global switch: simple-CPAT (basic CPAT equations for every sector, power included), standard-CPAT (engineering power and transport models on), CPAT partial adjustment, CES partial adjustment (taking the CES-compatible price of the energy service), and CDPM (SISEPUEDE) plus FTT-like. Excel-AI implements its core equations as LAMBDA formulas; the Python forms play the same role. Only the Excel-AI form is built now.
Keep the existing, clean folder structure of coded/ as the starting point; do not clutter the core folders with working files; prefer a subfolder (with one pointer file at the top) over more than three new files in a folder. Recommend improvements to the structure, then make them.



1.7 Sequence of work

Plan the folder and code structure for readability (this document, NORMS.md, the diagrams).
The equation list (Greek letters) and its parallel version with code names.
Design choices: documented here (section 10) and gone through with the user, question by question.
The detailed plan (section 11 and coded/TODO.md), then the build.

title: Appendix G — Specification and design decisions
text:
2. Principles

Follow Excel-AI. The numbers of Coded CPAT equal Excel-AI’s, code by code, year by year; a difference is a defect of one of the two, found and registered. Through Excel-AI, Coded CPAT inherits the replication rule (never replicate a legacy bug; replicate and track every legacy issue).
Readable first. One equation, one function, with the equation in the docstring as in the equation list; names from the codes map; no hidden constants; the model order written once (mitigation/chain.py). Speed comes second, and is reached by working on whole arrays of countries and scenarios at once, not by obscure code.
One model, many front ends. One entry point, cpat_model.run(scenarios, database, settings), used by the command line (scenario files, many countries and scenarios), the Shiny app (one country, two or more scenarios, reactive) and the tests.
Same inputs, same data, same codes as Excel-AI. Scenario inputs are MTInputs rows by NameOfParameter; advanced inputs are the legacy Manual inputs, Settings and Constants; data come from the same databases; results carry the Excel-AI output codes.
Structure that allows change. The core demand equations sit behind slots that the scenario input ModelForm can fill with other forms (D4); downstream modules (distribution, air pollution, transport co-benefits) talk to mitigation through declared interfaces.
Documents from one source. qmd for people, generated Word copies, md for guides; the equation list in one source file for both of its versions.

title: Appendix G — Specification and design decisions
text:
3. Folder structure

3.1 Principles

Keep what is clean. The top level of coded/ stays as it is: cpat_model/ (the model), cpat_shiny/ (the app), cpat_testing/ (tests), cpat_documentation/ (documents), and the entry points and configuration files. Only NORMS.md is added at the top.
The package reads like the model. Inside cpat_model/, one subpackage per block of Excel-AI, named for what it computes, and one file, mitigation/chain.py, that lists the blocks in the order they run. A reader learns the model by reading chain.py, then each block in turn.
Shared machinery in one place (core/), the switchable equation forms in another (forms/), so model blocks hold only equations.
Inputs and data at the edge. Only inputs/ reads scenario files and only data/ reads databases; model code receives arrays.
Documents in cpat_documentation/, one subfolder per kind (project, equations, developer, user), with qmd sources and generated Word copies.
No working files in the core folders (NORMS 2.2): kept comparison scripts in cpat_testing/compare/, run outputs in coded/outputs/ (git-ignored).

title: Appendix G — Specification and design decisions
text:
4. How a run works

4.1 From inputs to results





flowchart LR
  subgraph IN[Inputs]
    SC["Scenario set<br/>(MTInputs rows x scenarios)"]
    UI["Shiny app<br/>(same table, in memory)"]
    ADV["Advanced inputs<br/>(time series, Manual inputs, Settings)"]
  end
  subgraph DB[Databases]
    FULL["full<br/>(private repository)"]
    PUB["public<br/>(no proprietary tables)"]
    DUM["dummy"]
  end
  RUN["cpat_model.run()<br/>countries x scenarios"]
  RES["Results<br/>by Excel-AI output code<br/>country x scenario x year"]
  OUT1["Shiny charts and tables"]
  OUT2["Excel-style export"]
  OUT3["Comparisons<br/>Excel-AI, legacy CPAT"]
  SC --> RUN
  UI --> RUN
  ADV --> RUN
  FULL -.-> RUN
  PUB --> RUN
  DUM -.-> RUN
  RUN --> RES
  RES --> OUT1
  RES --> OUT2
  RES --> OUT3








4.2 Two passes, three stages (D1, D15: recommended options)
Excel-AI computes year by year with no circular reference: year t reads year t-1 and earlier (the GDP feedback reaches year t+1; power demand reads last year’s electricity price; capacity, vintages and vehicle stocks are recursions on t-1), and its only look-aheads read exogenous paths (the levelised variable cost of power over [t, 2041], built from prices and policies; next year’s manual capacity input). Policy scenarios also read scenario-1 values: stored ones (sheet BaselineCO2: CO2 by ETS sector, the calibration values in the GHG inventory year) and same-year ones (.ref, which reach the model only through the fiscal space and so GDP of t+1). Coded CPAT therefore runs the baseline first, then each policy scenario in turn (any number of scenarios; D15), each run in three stages:





flowchart TB
  subgraph PASS1["First the baseline (scenario 1), all countries"]
    direction TB
    P1["PREPARE"] --> L1["YEAR LOOP"] --> F1["FINISH"]
  end
  STORE["Baseline values the policy scenarios read<br/>(CO2 by ETS sector, calibration in the inventory year,<br/>.ref values of each year)"]
  subgraph PASS2["Then each policy scenario 2..n in turn, all countries"]
    direction TB

title: Appendix G — Specification and design decisions
text:
7. Switchable equation forms
The behavioural core of CPAT is a small number of equations: fuel demand by sector and fuel, electricity demand, power supply (dispatch and investment) and road transport. Excel-AI implements each as a named LAMBDA (FUELUSE and AEEIFACTOR for fuel demand, DEMANDMULT for electricity, DISPATCH, LOGITW, FIRSTROUND, CHEAPFILL, LEVELISED for power, ROADSWITCH, DEMROAD, OWNDEM, GOMPTGT for road transport).
The switch is a scenario input (D4). A new input ModelForm is added at the end of the MTInputs rows (below the last legacy row, in the block of prototype additions, root NORMS section 4), the same in Excel-AI’s ScenarioDefinition and in Coded CPAT’s scenario sets, one value per scenario. In Excel-AI the LAMBDA of each core equation reads it; in Python the block calls a slot in cpat_model/forms/, and ModelForm decides which implementation fills it.
The existing selectors stay as they are. The engineer-or-elasticity selectors of power and road transport (TrModel, and the power model choice) are unchanged and are not overridden by ModelForm; power always uses the engineer model. ModelForm chooses the form of the demand equations:








ModelForm
Fuel and electricity demand
Status




CPAT (default)
CPAT constant elasticities (Excel-AI FUELUSE, DEMANDMULT)
Built first: replicates Excel-AI


CPAT partial adjustment
Partial adjustment towards the CPAT long-run level (issue I62)
Later


CES partial adjustment
CES demand for energy services with partial adjustment, taking the CES-compatible price of each service
Later


CDPM-FTT
CDPM (SISEPUEDE)-like stock model with FTT-like technology diffusion
Later



“Simple-CPAT” and “standard-CPAT” of the original request are then the CPAT form with the elasticity or engineer selectors of road transport (and, if it is ever built, of power).
Rules: every implementation of a slot has the same signature (year t and t-1 values in, year t values out); a new form never changes the numbers of CPAT; a form that needs new parameters takes them from the advanced inputs, with defaults that leave CPAT unchanged; the row is added to Excel-AI and Python in the same release.

text:
10. Design choices: decided (user 2026-10-29)
The user went through the choices on 2026-10-29. The table gives each decision; the options considered follow it, for the record. coded/NORMS.md states the rules that follow.








#
Choice
Decision (user 2026-10-29)




D1
Order of computation
Year by year: prepare (quantity-free, all years) → year loop (every mitigation block, then the air-pollution and transport co-benefit modules, then GDP) → finish


D2
How quantities are held
xarray labelled arrays (country, year, fuel, sector, …)


D3
Variable names
CPAT code stems (ener, atp, …), with a registry from the codes map


D4
Switch between equation forms
A new scenario input ModelForm, added at the end of the MTInputs rows, set up the same way in Excel-AI and Python. It does not affect or override the existing engineer-or-elasticity selectors of power and transport (power always uses the engineer model)


D5
Input files
Scenario set as an MTInputs table (rows by NameOfParameter, a column per scenario, each scenario for a list of countries) plus an advanced-inputs workbook


D6
Databases
CSV folders in the current data/ structure, augmented by the input files; Coded CPAT reads tidy CSV (data/Public01/tidy/), with two-way converters to and from the legacy layout Excel-AI reads (user 2026-10-29); document the code interface (the tables, columns and keys the model reads, not a user interface) for the data person. Databases: full (private repository; used for comparisons where available) and dummy (data_old/dummy/, every table dummy)


D7
Existing code
Rebuild inside coded/, block by block; delete each old part when its replacement passes


D8
Comparison source
The existing Python recomputations first (excel_ai/mitigation/check_full.py, power_model_ref.py, transport_model_ref.py, distribution_ref.py), then Excel-AI values by code


D9
Time window
As Excel-AI, as run settings (base year, last year 2041)


D10
Placeholder modules
Two hooks: prepare (Excel-AI’s typed values, which feed the Pigouvian taxes) and step(t) in the year loop (empty until the module is built)


D11
Performance
Under 1 second for the user interface (one country, two scenarios)


D12
Website
One Quarto site at docs/, tabs CPAT methodology, Excel-AI, Coded CPAT


D13
Equation list source
One source (equations.yaml), both versions generated


D14
Versioning
Based on Excel-AI: <Excel-AI version>p<Python version>, e.g. 0.9.1p0.1 = Python version 0.1 of the replication of Excel-AI 0.9.1. Excel-AI’s numbering was rebased on 2026-10-29 (mitigation 9.0 is now 0.9.0, distribution 1.3 is 0.1.3), so the first release replicating today’s Excel-AI is 0.9.0p0.1


D15
Baseline values read by policy scenarios
n scenarios, run scenario by scenario: the baseline pass first, then each policy scenario in turn, reading the baseline values it needs


D16
Scenario inputs acting as global settings
Run settings, taken from the baseline column, with a check that warns when another scenario column differs




Structure and computation
D1. Order of computation: year by year, or module by module? (decided: see the table)

A. Year by year, all modules within the year (recommended). Three stages: prepare (all years at once, for everything without feedback: policy paths, international prices, deflators, exogenous drivers, base-year calibration), the year loop (for t = base year + 1 … last year, every block of mitigation, then air pollution and transport co-benefits, for year t; GDP of year t feeds year t+1), finish (all-year results, welfare, indicators; distribution in its analysis year). This is how Excel-AI computes (years across, each year reads the year before; GDP feedback one year later, NORMS 5c), so the numbers match by construction, and later modules with feedback (Pigouvian taxes from air-pollution damages, endogenous transport) fit without restructuring.
B. Module by module, each over all years at once (vectorised in time). Simpler for blocks without feedback, but the GDP feedback and the lagged price terms force iterations over the whole model until convergence; harder to match Excel-AI exactly.
C. Hybrid by module: modules without feedback over all years, the rest year by year. Two styles in one code base; less readable.

D2. How quantities are held in the code (decided: see the table)

A. Labelled arrays, xarray (recommended). Each quantity is an array with named dimensions (country, scenario, year, fuel, sector, …). Equations read like the equation list (ener = ener_prev * (atp / atp_prev) ** eps_u), broadcasting by name; many countries and scenarios cost nothing extra. One added dependency.
B. pandas DataFrames with a MultiIndex (today’s coded/): familiar, but index alignment and year columns as strings make equations long.
C. numpy arrays with axis conventions: fastest, least readable.

D3. Variable names in the code (decided: see the table)

A. CPAT code stems (recommended): ener, atp, ctx, with _prev, _ref, _chg suffixes; a generated variable registry (from the codes map) gives description, unit, dimensions and Greek symbol. Matches Excel-AI and the outputs one to one; the codes are short but documented in every docstring.
B. Descriptive English names (fuel_use, after_tax_price) with the code as metadata: easier for a newcomer, but two vocabularies to keep aligned.

D4. The switch between equation forms (decided: see the table)

A. One global setting model_form, mapped to a form for each core-equation slot (recommended). Slots: fuel demand, electricity demand, power supply, road transport, service price (CES-compatible price). Forms: simple_cpat (elasticity equations for every sector, power and road included), standard_cpat (Excel-AI: engineering power and road models on; default), cpat_partial_adjustment, ces_partial_adjustment, cdpm_ftt (SISEPUEDE-like stock model plus FTT-like technology diffusion). Each form is a function with the same signature, registered in cpat_model/forms/, as Excel-AI’s LAMBDAs. Only standard_cpat (and the switches Excel-AI already has, e.g. TrModel) is built now.
B. As A, plus an override per slot or per sector (e.g. CES in buildings only). Can be added later without changing A.
Question: should the scenario inputs that already switch models in Excel-AI and legacy (road transport TrModel, power) stay per-scenario inputs, with model_form only setting their defaults? (recommended: yes)

D5. Input files (decided: see the table)

A. Scenario set: one table (xlsx or CSV), rows = the legacy MTInputs rows in order (NameOfParameter), columns = scenarios, plus a row per scenario for the country (or “all”); Excel-AI’s ScenarioDefinition pastes into it. Advanced inputs: one workbook with one tab per kind (time series by year, tables by fuel and sector, settings), defaults from Excel-AI Settings, Manual inputs and Constants. The Shiny app writes the same structures in memory.
B. YAML/JSON scenario files (one per scenario). Readable for programmers, but not the MTInputs form people use.
Question: can one scenario set mix countries (scenario x country pairs), or is a scenario always “these inputs for every listed country”? (recommended: inputs per scenario, applied to a list of countries; country-specific values through the advanced inputs)

D6. Databases (decided: see the table)

A. A database is a folder of CSV tables plus a manifest (datapackage.json: tables, columns, source, licence class, proprietary or not). public in this repository (data/), full in the private repository (same layout, the four proprietary tables added), dummy as today. The model reads DATA_ENVIRONMENT (public, full, dummy) and the path of the private repository from .env. Excel-AI’s data workbook is built from the same database (data_old/scripts/build_data_workbook.py), so both models read identical numbers.
B. A single database file (SQLite or DuckDB) per set. One file to move, fast queries; but binary, not diff-able in git.
Answered (user 2026-10-29): (i) the four proprietary tables are EnergyCons/Balances, Prices_dom, IO_GTAP and HHSurvey; (ii) the systematic comparisons use the private full database where it is available, and the code must also allow dummy as an option; (iii) every table in data_old/dummy/ is dummy (not only the four), so a real public set (full minus the four tables) is not yet in this repository. Still open: where the public set lives and whether it is needed beyond full and dummy (see the design questions).

D7. The existing code in coded/ (decided: see the table)

A. Keep the folders, rebuild the model inside them block by block (recommended). cpat_shiny/, cpat_testing/, cpat_documentation/ and the data loaders stay; cpat_model/mitigation/ is rebuilt in Excel-AI block order on the new structure (D1-D4); each old subpackage is deleted when its replacement passes the Excel-AI comparison. Distribution (validated against Excel, 48 tests) is moved onto the new structure with its tests unchanged.
B. A new package next to the old one (e.g. cpat/), switch over at the end. Clean start, but two models in the repository for months.
C. Refactor the existing components in place. Least churn, but the existing design (pandas, component classes, input keys) shapes the new code.

D8. Excel-AI as the comparison source (decided: see the table)

A. Extract Excel-AI values by code (all codes, both scenario groups, every year) from the recalculated release workbook into a fixture table, one per release and country set, with a script in cpat_testing/compare/ (LibreOffice recalculation, as the Excel checks). Python compares code by code, tolerance 1e-9.
B. Compare against the existing Python recomputations of excel_ai/mitigation/check_full.py. Faster to start, but it is a second implementation, not Excel-AI itself.
Question: which countries for “all countries”: every country in the data, or a fixed test set?



Scope and behaviour
D9. The time window and base year (decided: see the table): base year and last year (2041) as settings, the same for all countries in a run.
D10. Placeholders for air pollution and transport co-benefits (decided: see the table)

A. Each module is a package with declared inputs (the codes it reads from mitigation: section 15 for air pollution, section 5b for transport co-benefits) and outputs (the codes it returns: air.vpm and concentration coefficients; tran.acc.km, tran.con.km, tran.rdm.km), and two hooks: prepare returns Excel-AI’s typed values (FromAirPollution, FromTransportCB), which feed the Pigouvian taxes before the year loop as in Excel-AI (I151); step(t) runs inside the year loop after the local pollutants and computes nothing until the module is built (section 4.5).
B. Post-processing only, after the run. Simpler, but the Pigouvian taxes need the values before the loop, and a later live module would need restructuring.
Question for later: when a live module’s damages depend on the scenario’s own emissions, should they feed prices with a one-year lag (acyclic, simple) or through an outer iteration (exact, slower)?

D11. Performance target for the Shiny app (decided: see the table): one country, two scenarios in about 1-2 seconds; all countries, a few scenarios, in minutes. Acceptable?
D12. The website (decided: see the table)

A. One Quarto website at docs/ with tabs: CPAT methodology (the existing book), Excel-AI (method notes, register), Coded CPAT (spec, equation list, developer guide). The Python pages stay in coded/cpat_documentation/ and the website lists them; Word copies are generated.
B. A separate website per project.

D13. Equation list source (decided: see the table)

A. One source, two documents. The equations are written once in equations/equations.yaml (id, part, core or adjustment, Greek form, code form, indices, meaning, methodology reference, Excel-AI reference); a script writes the Greek and the code-name qmd from it, so the two never drift apart, and the tests check that every id has a function.
B. Two hand-written qmd files.

D14. Release and versioning of Coded CPAT (decided: see the table): version numbers follow the Excel-AI version replicated (e.g. Coded CPAT 9.0 = Excel-AI 9.0), or an own version with the Excel-AI version stated?
D15. Baseline values read by policy scenarios (decided: see the table)

A. Two passes: run the baseline (scenario 1) for all years first, then every policy scenario together, reading the baseline values they need (CO2 by ETS sector, the calibration values in the GHG inventory year, the same-year .ref values). Numbers equal Excel-AI’s as long as its stored values are current (section 12, item 1); the comparison reports it if not.
B. Read Excel-AI’s stored values (sheet BaselineCO2) as data. Matches the shipped workbook exactly even when it is stale, but ties Python to a workbook.
C. One pass, all scenarios together, with stored values from a previous run (as Excel). Fastest, least transparent.

D16. Scenario inputs that act as global settings (decided: see the table): inputs that Excel-AI reads from the scenario-1 column for every scenario (BiomassLeakage, BiomassNormal, cooking exemption, cookstove efficiencies) become run settings (A), checked to agree across the scenario columns; or (B) stay per-scenario inputs with the baseline value used for all, as Excel-AI.

title: Appendix G — Specification and design decisions
text:
12. Excel-AI choices to flag
The overriding norm is to replicate Excel-AI. These choices are replicated as they are, but they are unusual enough that the user should know of them before the build; each is already in the register or proposed for it.

Stored scenario-1 values. Policy scenarios read baseline values stored on sheet BaselineCO2 and refreshed by the build (CO2 by ETS sector for the ETS cap and price estimate; the CO2 calibration factor and the energy-methane calibration in the GHG inventory year, 2024, which is after the base year). In Excel the results therefore depend on values stored by the last build, not on the current inputs. Coded CPAT computes them in its baseline pass (D15); the two agree only while Excel-AI’s stored values are current, which the comparison checks.
Scenario inputs that act as global settings. Some inputs are read from the scenario-1 column for every scenario (BiomassLeakage, BiomassNormal, the cooking-exemption inputs, cookstove efficiencies). In Coded CPAT they become run settings (D16), with a check that every scenario column agrees.
The road engineer model runs in every scenario whatever TrModel (issue I100); its outputs feed the transport co-benefit interface even when the elasticity form drives fuel use.
Module values typed for Egypt only. The air-pollution and transport co-benefit values (FromAirPollution, FromTransportCB) are typed from the legacy 465 run for Egypt; every other country reads 0 (I106), so Pigouvian taxes and those welfare terms are zero outside Egypt.
Pigouvian taxes by proxy (I151): marginal air-pollution damages use base-year fuel-use weights and typed values, so they do not respond to the scenario; this keeps the model acyclic (the tax enters the forward-looking power cost) and is the reason the placeholder modules feed the model in the prepare stage.
Fuel demand has no partial adjustment (I62): the full response to a price change happens in the year of the change. The cpat_partial_adjustment form addresses this later.
Investment need extrapolates required generation as Req(t)²/Req(t−1) instead of reading next year (L67 fix), and the levelised variable cost of power looks forward to 2041: both are exogenous, so they sit in the prepare stage.
ETS price by goal seek. The ETS permit price is found by an outer iteration over whole runs (run only on request); between runs it is a stored override row per scenario. Coded CPAT keeps the override as an advanced input and offers the iteration as a separate function.


12b. Apparent errors in the methodology documentation
Registered as documentation bugs DOC1-DOC20 (new code DOC, root NORMS section 0; excel_ai/BUGS.md section 3). Found while extracting the notation (full list: ../equations/reference/notation_from_methodology.md section 4). They do not change Coded CPAT, which follows Excel-AI, but the methodology should be corrected:

No in-model GDP equation: neither the multipliers chapter nor the mitigation chapter gives the GDP feedback; the equation list takes it from Excel-AI.
Undefined symbols: \(\epsilon_G\) in both power-demand equations (presumably \(\epsilon_Y\)); \(tex\) in Appendix C.
Markup sign: \(mu^T = gnc^{av} + tmc - hrp\) is then added to the price; to reproduce historical prices it must be \(hrp - gnc^{av} - tmc\).
Storage: the derivative of \(sst = 9v^2\) is written \(18v^2\) (should be \(18v\)); the long-term storage table does not match its formula.
Welfare: \(ddw\) uses \(nc\) for \(ncp\), and the text calls half the difference of the taxes their average.
Supply price: producer subsidies added in Appendix C, subtracted in the main text; base-year window 2019-2021 in one place, 2018-2022 in another.
Overloaded letters: \(g\) (sector group, generation, growth rate, consumption category, PIT gain), \(\gamma\) (six meanings), \(E\), \(p\)/\(P\), \(j\), \(i\); electricity coded ecy in mitigation and ely in distribution. The equation list fixes one meaning per letter within each part (its symbol appendix).

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
0. The overriding norm: follow Excel-AI
Source: coded/NORMS.md.
Rules for every task in coded/. They add to the repository-wide ../NORMS.md, of which these sections apply to Python as written: 0 (never replicate a legacy bug; always replicate a legacy issue, and track it), 4 (inputs: MTInputs rows and NameOfParameter names), 6, 6b (task completion: CAVEATS.md; norms follow the lessons), 7 (methodology and version notes are different documents) and 8 (data). Its Excel sections (1-3, 5: columns, style, LAMBDA encoding, releases) do not apply, except where this file points to them.
The design choices behind these rules (D1-D16) were decided by the user on 2026-10-29: spec cpat_documentation/project/Spec.qmd section 10. A rule citing Dn follows that decision.

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
Excel-AI is the specification. Coded CPAT replicates the mitigation and distribution modules of Excel-AI (../excel_ai/CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm, ../excel_ai/CPAT-AI-Distribution-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm) number for number. When the methodology (../docs/01_MainDocumentation/), legacy CPAT and Excel-AI disagree, the code follows Excel-AI and the difference is already, or is then, in the register.
Which version (D14). The version of Coded CPAT is <Excel-AI version>p<Python version>, e.g. 1.0.0p1.0: Python version 1.0 of the replication of Excel-AI 1.0.0 (Excel-AI’s numbering was rebased on 2026-10-29: mitigation 9.0 is 0.9.0, distribution 1.3 is 0.1.3). The package states both (EXCEL_AI_VERSION, __version__), and each module docstring the Excel-AI version it replicates. Moving to a new Excel-AI version is a task of its own: port the changed rows (the Excel version log and ../CAVEATS.md list them), then rerun the comparison.
Bugs are not replicated; issues are (user rules 2026-10-29; root NORMS.md section 0 rule 6). Coded CPAT follows Excel-AI everywhere except in its bugs. A prototype bug (M: Excel-AI does not compute what it means to) is never replicated: register it the same day (OPEN_PROTO_BUGS in ../excel_ai/mitigation/issues_register.py), add its fix to the Excel-AI TODO list (../excel_ai/plans/TODO.md), fix it here where the fix is obvious (a comment # bug M<n> fixed (Excel-AI: ...) at the line), list the codes that then differ from Excel-AI in cpat_testing/compare/known_differences.py (the tests check they differ), note it on TODO.md (section “Excel-AI bugs”) and tell the user. Where the fix is not obvious, keep Excel-AI’s formula (# Excel-AI bug M<n>, replicated until ...) and follow the prototype’s fixed version. An issue (a potential improvement) is logged for later and replicated for now. Never change Excel-AI’s behaviour silently.
Codes are shared. Variable codes, input names (NameOfParameter) and output codes are those of Excel-AI and the codes map ../excel_ai/CPAT-AI_CodesMap_v<version>.xlsx. Python never invents a second name for a quantity that has a code.
One register. Bugs and issues found while porting go in the one register (../excel_ai/mitigation/issues_register.py; root NORMS.md section 0 rule 3), with module “Coded CPAT” where only Python is affected. Coded CPAT keeps no list of its own.

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
1. Readability: equations, names, comments
The purpose of the code is that a person with the equation list open can find, read and check every equation.

One equation, one function. Each equation of the equation list (cpat_documentation/equations/) is one small function (or one clearly marked line in a short function), named after the quantity it computes. Its docstring starts with the equation id and the equation in the notation of the equation list, then the Excel-AI rows it replicates:
def ener(ener_prev, atp, atp_prev, ...):
    """EQ-M4.1  Fuel use, CPAT constant-elasticity form.

    Q_t = Q_{t-1} * (1 + g_t)^(eps_Y) * (P_t / P_{t-1})^(eps_U) * ...      (over fuels i, sectors j)
    Excel-AI: Mitigation section 6, code ener.<sector>.<fuel>; Equations.md E69.
    """
Names are CPAT codes (D3). A variable that has a code in the codes map is called by its code stem in the code (ener, atp, ctx); the previous year adds _prev, the baseline (scenario 1) value adds _ref, a change against the baseline _chg (as Excel-AI .ref, .chg). The variable registry (cpat_model/core/variables.py, generated from the codes map) gives each code its description, unit, dimensions and Greek symbol. Names without a code (local helpers) are plain English words in snake_case, never single letters other than the index letters of the equation list.
The equation list and the code agree. An equation added, removed or changed in the code is changed in the equation list in the same task, and the other way round. A test lists every equation id and fails if one has no function or one function cites an unknown id.
No hard-coded numbers. Apart from 0, 1 and array positions, every number comes from the inputs, the data or a named constant in cpat_model/core/constants.py with its source and unit (as root NORMS.md section 3, “No hard-coded constants”).
Units in the registry, conversions in one place. Money units follow the Excel-AI vocabulary (USD m, LCU bn, USD/GJ, real or nominal; root NORMS.md section 3, “Money units”). A function body does not multiply by 1e3, 1e6 or 1e9; it calls a named conversion.
Short and flat. A function that needs scrolling is split. No clever one-liners, no metaprogramming in model code, no inheritance deeper than one level. Prefer explicit arguments to reading a global state.
Comments say why, not what. The docstring says what; a comment explains a choice, an Excel-AI quirk (with its register code, e.g. # I85: percentages typed as whole numbers, as legacy) or a unit.

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
2. Where things go (folders and files)

The layout is in README.md and in the spec, section 3. Code goes in cpat_model/ (the model), cpat_shiny/ (the app), cpat_testing/ (tests); documents in cpat_documentation/. The top of coded/ holds only the entry points (run_model.py, app.py), configuration (.env, environment files; the settings are cpat_model/settings.py) and the three guides (README.md, NORMS.md, TODO.md).
No working files in the core folders. Scratch scripts, notebooks, exports and one-off comparisons do not go in cpat_model/, cpat_shiny/ or cpat_testing/. Comparison scripts that are kept go in cpat_testing/compare/; run outputs go in coded/outputs/ (git-ignored); anything else temporary stays outside the repository.
Folders, not long lists. A folder gets at most three new files in one task; more become a subfolder with one pointer file (a README.md or __init__.py that says what is inside).
The package follows the model. cpat_model/mitigation/ has one subpackage per Excel-AI block, named for what it computes (policies, prices, power, fuel_use, revenues, emissions, gdp, …), and one file, chain.py, that lists the order in which the blocks run (spec section 3). A reader learns the model order from that one file.
No Old/, tmp_, new_, _v2 files. Git keeps the history; a replaced file is deleted in the task that replaces it.
Data never in coded/. All data are in ../data/ (root NORMS.md section 8); test fixtures with their tests (cpat_testing/**/data_expected/).

title: Appendix H — Python norms
section: 3. Model structure: dimensions, the year loop, modules, equation forms
text:
3. Model structure: dimensions, the year loop, modules, equation forms

Labelled arrays (D2). Model quantities are labelled arrays (xarray) with named dimensions: country, year, and the dimensions of the quantity (fuel, sector, tech, user, decile, …), using the index names of the equation list. Equations broadcast by name; no positional axis arithmetic in model code.
Baseline first, then scenario by scenario; three stages (D1, D15). A run takes any number of scenarios. The baseline (scenario 1) runs first, then each policy scenario in turn, reading the baseline values it needs (as Excel-AI’s BaselineCO2 and .ref). Each scenario run has three stages: prepare (everything that depends on no model quantity, for all years at once: policy paths, international prices and the price chain, power cost paths including the levelised variable cost, exogenous drivers, the module values that feed Pigouvian taxes), the year loop (for each year t, every block in the order of chain.py, each reading only year t and earlier years: all of mitigation, then the air-pollution and transport co-benefit modules for year t, then the GDP effect that reaches t+1), and finish (all-year results: carbon-pricing indicators, welfare, exports; then distribution in its analysis year). No equation reads a later model year (root NORMS.md 5c, circular references, rule 1); a look-ahead on exogenous paths belongs in prepare.
Countries together, scenarios in turn. Every function works for any number of countries at once (an array dimension); nothing loops over countries in model code. Scenarios run one after another (core/loop.py is the only scenario loop) and their results are joined along a scenario dimension. Scenario 1 is the baseline; _ref values are read from the baseline run in the same year, as Excel-AI’s ref_formula. Inputs that Excel-AI reads from the baseline column for every scenario are run settings, checked for agreement (D16).
Modules talk through declared interfaces. Each module declares what it reads and what it writes (codes). Downstream modules (distribution, air pollution, transport co-benefits) read only their declared inputs, as the Excel modules read only FromMitigation (root NORMS.md section 3, “Exports to modules”).
Switchable equation forms (D4). The demand equations (fuel demand, electricity demand, the CES service price) are called through the slots of cpat_model/forms/, never directly. The form is a scenario input, ModelForm, the last MTInputs row, set up the same way in Excel-AI and Python; the default, CPAT, is the Excel-AI form and the only one built until the user asks for another. ModelForm does not override the existing engineer-or-elasticity selectors of road transport and power (power always uses the engineer model). A new form never changes the numbers of CPAT, and is added to Excel-AI and Python in the same release.
Placeholder modules (D10). Air pollution and transport co-benefits each have prepare (Excel-AI’s typed module values, which feed the Pigouvian taxes) and step(t) (in the year loop after the local pollutants; empty until the module is built).

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
4. Inputs: scenarios and advanced inputs

Scenario inputs are MTInputs (D5). A scenario set is a table with the rows of legacy MTInputs (NameOfParameter, root NORMS.md section 4; the Excel-AI additions, ModelForm last, below them) and one column per scenario, each scenario run for a list of countries; the Shiny app builds the same table. Input keys are the NameOfParameter names, in legacy units (I85).
Advanced inputs (time series and longer-form inputs, the legacy Manual inputs tab and Excel-AI Settings) come from one advanced-inputs workbook per run (a tab per kind: time series, Manual inputs blocks, Settings, Constants; D5), with defaults from Excel-AI. Input files live in ../data/inputs/ (D6).
Validated once. Inputs are read and checked (names known, types, ranges, option values as legacy) in cpat_model/inputs/ before the model runs; model code never reads a raw input file.

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
5. Data: databases

Databases (D6; user 2026-10-29: tidy CSV). Coded CPAT reads tidy CSV (../data/Public01/tidy/: one table per file, long, standard keys, country ISO3 upper case), converted both ways from the legacy layout Excel-AI reads by ../data/scripts/tidy_convert.py (exact round trip, tested). A database is a folder of tidy tables with its _layout/, in the structure of ../data/ (input files under ../data/inputs/). Two exist: full (every table, including the four proprietary tables EnergyCons/Balances, Prices_dom, IO_GTAP, HHSurvey; a private repository, never this one) and dummy (../data/Public01/tidy/, the default: the public legacy tables plus the Egypt rows of the proprietary tables that the public legacy file contains; the older ../data_old/dummy/ is every table dummy and no longer read). The code interface (each table, column, key and unit the model reads) is documented for the data person in ../data_old/INTERFACE.md, and a loader reads nothing it does not list. The choice is a setting (.env: DATA_ENVIRONMENT, the path of the full database outside the repository). The systematic comparisons use full where it is available, with dummy as the option that always works (user 2026-10-29); every model in a comparison reads the same database.
Never commit proprietary data, nor results computed from them (root NORMS.md section 8).
Loaders read, never compute. cpat_model/data/ loads and reshapes tables to the model’s dimensions; any calculation on data is a model equation with an id.

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
6. Results and codes

Results are keyed by Excel-AI output codes (<variable>.<sector>.<fuel> as the prototype) and dimensions country, scenario, year, so every Python result can be set against the Excel-AI row with the same code.
Results belong to the scenario; differences as Excel-AI (root NORMS.md section 3c: x.ref, x.chg, x.pct only for strictly positive quantities; price changes are price indices; ratios from summed levels).

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
7. Tests and comparisons

Three levels. Unit tests per equation (small hand-checked cases); block tests against reference values by code for one country: first the existing Python recomputations of Excel-AI (../excel_ai/mitigation/check_full.py, power_model_ref.py, transport_model_ref.py, distribution_ref.py; D8), then values extracted from the recalculated Excel-AI workbook (directly for the rows the recomputations lack); end-to-end comparisons (all codes, then all countries).
Tolerance. Python equals Excel-AI to a relative difference of 1e-9 (absolute 1e-9 near zero) unless a difference is explained and registered.
Comparison order: Python against Excel-AI, one country (Egypt), then all countries; Python or Excel-AI against legacy CPAT, one country, then all; always on the systematic dataset (section 5).
Speed (D11). One country with two scenarios runs in under 1 second for the user interface (data and the baseline run cached). Speed never costs readability: it comes from array operations and caching.
pytest passes before every commit. A failing comparison is not skipped or loosened to pass; it is fixed or registered.

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
8. Documents: qmd, Word, the website

qmd is the source. Documents for people (spec, plan, design choices, equation list, method notes) are Quarto markdown (.qmd) in cpat_documentation/; Word copies (.docx) are generated from them (cpat_documentation/make_docs.py), never edited by hand. Guides for agents and developers (README.md, NORMS.md, TODO.md) stay .md: GitHub shows them formatted, every tool reads them, and Quarto renders .md as well as .qmd, so they can join the website unchanged.
Diagrams are mermaid blocks in the qmd (Quarto draws them); make_docs.py renders them to PNG for Word.
Notation. The equation list uses the Greek letters and index letters of the methodology (../docs/01_MainDocumentation/); where the methodology has none, it says so and uses the Excel-AI note (../excel_ai/mitigation/Equations.md). Its code version uses the codes map.
Methodology, not history (root NORMS.md section 7): the equation list and method notes describe the current model only.
The documentation book (user 2026-10-29). The Coded CPAT documentation is a Quarto book, the website’s Coded CPAT tab, in the style of the methodology documentation: Part I what you need to know (concise: quick start, the database first, scenarios, results, editing, testing), Part II how it works, the complete reference in appendices. Chapters are written in cpat_documentation/guide/; the appendices are generated from the code and data (../docs/CPAT_coded_documentation_qmd/make_qmd.py). A task that changes how to run, edit or test the model, the database, the inputs or the results updates its chapter the same day; a task that changes the tests reruns make_qmd.py --tests (the test status) before quarto render.

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
9. Task completion and bookkeeping
As root NORMS.md section 6: every finished task gets a ../CAVEATS.md entry; open work is in TODO.md (tick it, add the follow-ups); a lesson with a cause that can repeat becomes a norm here, with its check (root section 6b).

title: Appendix H — Python norms
text:
10. Python conventions

Python 3.12, pandas, numpy, xarray (environment.yml, requirements.txt); new dependencies only with a reason in the task’s CAVEATS.md entry.
Type hints on public functions; ruff for lint and format.
Functions are pure: inputs in, results out, no file or global state inside model code. Reading files happens in cpat_model/data/ and cpat_model/inputs/ only.
The one public entry point is cpat_model.run(...) (spec section 3); run_model.py, the Shiny app and the tests all call it.

title: Appendix J — Glossary
text:
Term
Meaning




Baseline
Scenario 1: no new policies; every other scenario is compared with it


Block
One part of the Mitigation sheet, one function or module in mitigation/


Bug (M, L)
A model does not compute what it means to. Prototype bugs (M) and legacy bugs (L) are fixed, never copied


Code (output code)
The name of a result row, shared with Excel-AI: egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2


Coded CPAT
This Python model


Data step
A computation Excel-AI does on its Inputs sheet from the data, before the model rows


Dummy database
data/tidy/ in this repository: public data and dummy proprietary tables


Excel-AI
The Excel prototypes of CPAT-AI, generated by Python builders (excel_ai/)


Full database
Every country and the proprietary tables; a private repository


Issue (I)
A potential improvement: logged and copied as it is for now


Known difference
A code where Coded CPAT differs from Excel-AI because it fixes a bug still open in the prototype


Legacy CPAT
The original CPAT workbook (CPAT 1.0pre_465)


NameOfParameter
The name of an input in Excel-AI’s ScenarioDefinition sheet


REFCOL
Excel-AI’s reference to the baseline’s value of the same row and year


Scenario set
A table of inputs, one column per scenario, baseline first


Tidy CSV
One table per file, long, keys then value
